review_status: DRAFT. An agronomist or extension officer must check every line before field use. Hindi and Telugu text is a machine draft for native-speaker review.
scope_note: Tomato only. Pesticide options come from the NIPHM AESA-based IPM package for tomato (an older edition). Products from that package that may be banned or restricted (phorate, carbofuran, dimethoate, malathion, oxydemeton-methyl) were left out as a precaution; this was not a verified legal check. Confirm every entry, and every omission, against the current CIB&RC registered list before field use. Doses are reference doses only; the current registered label always overrides this file. Organic and biological options are left out for now by design.

Mild: Remove the worst affected leaves and keep them away from the plot (do not compost them).
Look at the same plants again in 3 to 5 days to see if it is spreading.
Wash your hands and tools after touching affected plants, and avoid working among wet plants.
Moderate: Remove affected leaves and check the plants around them for the same signs.
Start the control steps for this problem below, beginning with the farm-practice (cultural) measures.
If you use any spray, use only products approved locally for this crop and follow the label. Ask your extension officer if unsure.
Severe: Contact your agriculture extension officer today and show them this photo.
Isolate or remove badly affected plants so they do not infect others. Do not carry sap from sick plants to healthy ones on hands or tools.
Do not take seed, cuttings or seedlings from this plot.

Tomato healthy.summary: The leaf looks healthy. This does not rule out pests on other parts of the plant or problems that are not visible yet.

pests_to_check.name: Fruit borer caterpillars (Helicoverpa)
pests_to_check.why: young caterpillars eat leaves, then bore round holes into fruit

pests_to_check.name: Tobacco caterpillar (Spodoptera)
pests_to_check.why: scrapes leaves, then makes irregular holes and can strip the plant

pests_to_check.name: Whitefly
pests_to_check.why: small white flies under leaves; they carry leaf curl virus

pests_to_check.name: Serpentine leaf miner
pests_to_check.why: thin winding tunnels inside the leaf

pests_to_check.name: Thrips and spider mites
pests_to_check.why: bronzing or speckled leaves; mites make fine webbing in hot dry weather

Healthy: Scout once a week: pick 5 spots in the field and check 5 plants at each spot, looking under the leaves and at the shoot tips.
Hang yellow sticky traps just above the plants to watch for whitefly (4 to 5 per acre), and blue traps for thrips.
Put up pheromone traps (4 to 5 per acre) to watch for fruit borer and tobacco caterpillar moths.
Keep the field and nursery free of weeds and old crop residue.
If you see pests or damage, switch to Pest scan and take a close photo.

area_guidance.small_plot: Check every plant when you water.
area_guidance.field: Walk a zigzag across the field and check a few plants at each stop.

Tomato healthy.escalate_if: You see sudden wilting, many curled or spotted leaves, or insects in large numbers.
prevention: Raise seedlings on raised beds or in trays so that water drains away.
Use healthy seed and seedlings, and rotate tomato with a cereal crop such as maize or sorghum.
Grow 4 rows of maize or sorghum around the field as a guard crop.
sources: NIPHM / DPPQS, Govt. of India: AESA based IPM Package No. 18 - Tomato (niphm.gov.in/IPMPackages/Tomato.pdf)

Tomato Brown Spots.summary: Brown or dark spots on the leaf. Several diseases look alike at this stage, such as bacterial spot and fungal leaf spots, and the app cannot tell which one it is.

pests_to_check.name: No special insect vector
pests_to_check.why: bacterial spot and Septoria spread by rain splash, wind, infected seed and plant debris, and on hands and clothes

pests_to_check.name: Leaf miner and chewing insects
pests_to_check.why: wounds from insects can help germs enter, so check for tunnels and holes

effects_if_untreated: Spots join together, leaves turn yellow and drop.
With fewer leaves the plant makes less food, so fruit is smaller and can get sunscald.
Rain splash and overhead watering carry the problem to nearby plants.
Spots on fruit lower its market value.

Mild: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves.
Stake or prune so air can move between plants.
Moderate: Do not work in the plot while leaves are wet, and wash hands and tools after touching spotted plants.
Remove heavily spotted lower leaves first and destroy them.
Ask the extension officer to confirm if it is bacterial spot or a fungal leaf spot such as Septoria; the spray choice is different.
Severe: Ask the extension officer to confirm exactly which disease it is, because the right treatment depends on whether it is bacterial or fungal.
Do not save seed from these plants.

area_guidance.small_plot: Check every plant and remove affected leaves by hand.
area_guidance.field: Check plants at several spots across the field in a zigzag and count how many show spots. If many do, ask the extension officer about treating the whole field.

Tomato Brown Spots.escalate_if: Spots are on the fruit, spreading fast after rain, or more than a few plants are affected.
prevention: Rotate with non-host crops and do not leave old plant debris in the field.
Remove weeds such as black nightshade, which can carry the disease.

chemical_options.name: Mancozeb 75% WP
chemical_options.dose: 600 to 800 g in 300 l of water per acre

chemical_options.name: Streptocycline (streptomycin sulphate 9% + tetracycline hydrochloride 1% SP)
chemical_options.use_for: bacterial leaf spot only (not for fungal spots)
chemical_options.dose: 40 to 100 ppm solution (ask your extension officer how much to mix per tank); two sprays: one on the seed bed before transplanting and one in the main field after transplanting

sources: NIPHM / DPPQS, Govt. of India: AESA based IPM Package No. 18 - Tomato (niphm.gov.in/IPMPackages/Tomato.pdf)
Doses are the reference per-acre doses printed in that package. Check the current CIB&RC registered label before use.

Tomato blight leaf.display: Tomato leaf blight (early or late blight)
Tomato blight leaf.summary: Large brown patches, often with yellow edges. Early blight and late blight look similar in a photo. Late blight can spread very fast in cool, wet, cloudy weather.

pests_to_check.name: No special insect vector
pests_to_check.why: spores travel on wind, rain water, insects, workers and machinery

effects_if_untreated: Leaves die and drop, which exposes fruit to sunburn.
In cool wet weather late blight can reach stems and fruit and destroy a crop within days.
Spores travel on wind and rain to neighbouring fields.

Mild: Remove affected lower leaves and keep leaves dry.
Avoid overhead watering; give light irrigation.
Moderate: Destroy weeds and volunteer tomato plants, which can carry the disease.
Check neighbouring plants every day and watch the weather: warm, rainy and wet days make it spread faster.
If it keeps spreading after 3 to 5 days, ask your extension officer about the spray options below.
Severe: Act the same day: contact the extension officer.
Remove heavily infected plants and destroy them away from the field.
Warn neighbouring farmers, because spores travel by wind and water.

area_guidance.small_plot: Inspect every plant daily during wet weather.
area_guidance.field: Inspect field edges and low damp corners first, where blight usually starts.

Tomato blight leaf.escalate_if: New patches appear every day, stems or fruit are affected, or the weather is cool and wet.
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties if your seed supplier or KVK recommends one.
Change the nursery bed location every season and keep it free of weeds.
Do not plant tomato next to an older tomato or potato crop; rotate with non-host crops.
Keep the field clean: remove crop residue and weeds that can host the disease after harvest.

chemical_options.name: Mancozeb 75% WP
chemical_options.dose: 600 to 800 g in 300 l of water per acre

chemical_options.name: Azoxystrobin 23% SC
chemical_options.dose: 200 ml in 200 l of water per acre

chemical_options.name: Copper oxychloride 50% WP
chemical_options.dose: 1000 g in 300 to 400 l of water per acre

chemical_options.name: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP
chemical_options.dose: 600 g in 200 to 300 l of water per acre

sources: NIPHM / DPPQS, Govt. of India: AESA based IPM Package No. 18 - Tomato (niphm.gov.in/IPMPackages/Tomato.pdf)
Doses are the reference per-acre doses printed in that package. Check the current CIB&RC registered label before use.

Tomato virus.summary: Curled, yellowed or mottled leaves and stunted growth point to a virus such as leaf curl or mosaic. A plant that is infected cannot be cured.

pests_to_check.name: Whitefly
pests_to_check.why: spreads leaf curl virus; look under young leaves and shake the plant to see small white flies

pests_to_check.name: No insect for mosaic
pests_to_check.why: mosaic spreads on hands, clothes, tools, plant debris and seed

effects_if_untreated: Infected plants stay small and give few flowers and little fruit.
The plant becomes a source: whiteflies pick up the virus and carry it to healthy plants.
Whitefly honeydew can grow black sooty mould that blocks sunlight.
Plants infected when young lose the most yield.

Mild: Remove and destroy infected plants early. Do not leave them in the field.
Remove weeds nearby that can carry the virus or whiteflies.
Wash hands and tools after touching infected plants. Do not touch healthy plants after sick ones.
Moderate: Control whiteflies: hang yellow sticky cards (about 10 per acre) near the plants.
Do not plant new seedlings next to infected plants.
Ask the extension officer about the whitefly spray options below.
Severe: Remove the infected plants and talk to the extension officer about whitefly control for the whole area and virus-tolerant varieties for the next season.

area_guidance.small_plot: Remove infected plants and, if you can, cover seedlings with fine net.
area_guidance.field: Check the field borders first, where whiteflies enter, and mark patches of infected plants.

Tomato virus.escalate_if: More than a few plants show it, young plants are affected, or whiteflies are present in large numbers.
prevention: Raise seedlings in the nursery under a fine insect-proof net so whiteflies cannot reach them.
Grow maize or sorghum around the field as a barrier crop, to keep whiteflies out.
Use seed from healthy plants, rinse and dry it in shade, and remove infected seedlings before transplanting.
Ask your KVK or seed supplier about leaf-curl-tolerant varieties (NIPHM lists Arka Ananya, Kashi Vishesh, Kashi Amrit, COTH 2 and TNAU Hybrid Co3).
Do not grow tomato after tobacco, potato, chilli, capsicum or brinjal.

chemical_options.name: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL
chemical_options.use_for: whitefly (carries leaf curl); can also be used as a 15-minute seedling root dip before transplanting
chemical_options.dose: 60 to 70 ml in 200 l of water per acre

chemical_options.name: Thiamethoxam 25% WG
chemical_options.dose: 80 g in 200 l of water per acre

chemical_options.name: Spiromesifen 22.9% SC
chemical_options.dose: 250 ml in 200 l of water per acre

sources: NIPHM / DPPQS, Govt. of India: AESA based IPM Package No. 18 - Tomato (niphm.gov.in/IPMPackages/Tomato.pdf)
Doses are the reference per-acre doses printed in that package. Check the current CIB&RC registered label before use.
